entry: War crime in which U.S. Army soldiers killed between 347 and 504 civilians, almost all women, children and elderly men, in Sơn Mỹ village, [[South Vietnam]], on March 16, 1968. Troops had expected to confront a [[Viet Cong]] battalion that was not there. Female victims, including children as young as 12, were gang-raped and mutilated. The massacre was first reported as a victory and covered up. Journalist Seymour Hersh and veteran Ronald Ridenhour made it public in November 1969, prompting global outrage. Only Lieutenant William Calley Jr. was convicted, of murdering 22 villagers. It was the largest massacre by U.S. soldiers in the 20th century.

[[Toy|Toy line]] and media franchise of colorful [[Pony|ponies]], developed by American company Hasbro. The first line ran from 1982 until 1992 in the United States, selling 150 million pony toys during that decade before Hasbro discontinued it. The brand was revived in 1997, 2003 and 2010. The fourth incarnation, centered on the animated series *My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic*, gained a cult following among adult men. Retail sales exceeded $1 billion a year in 2014 and 2015. A fifth incarnation launched in 2021.

1988 Japanese animated fantasy film written and directed by [[Hayao Miyazaki]] and animated by [[Studio Ghibli]]. Two sisters move with their father to the countryside in 1950s Japan, where they befriend forest spirits, including the titular creature Totoro. Its themes include [[Animism|animism]], [[Shinto]] symbolism, [[Environmentalism|environmentalism]] and childhood. Released by [[Toho]], it grossed over $41 million worldwide and won the Animage Anime Grand Prix and Mainichi Film Award. Totoro is the mascot of Studio Ghibli.

Disabling chronic illness marked by profound fatigue that rest does not relieve. The hallmark symptom is post-exertional malaise, a worsening of symptoms after minor physical or mental activity that can last days or months. Other symptoms include sleep and memory problems, [[Pain|pain]] and dizziness when upright. The cause is unknown, and the illness often starts after an [[Infection|infection]]. No verified diagnostic test exists, and no approved treatment addresses the cause. Before the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], it affected two to nine out of every 1,000 people, depending on diagnostic criteria. It occurs more often in women, and about a quarter of those affected cannot leave their bed or home.

Armed conflict in [[Myanmar]] that began with the military coup of February 1, 2021. The seizure of power triggered mass protests and a violent crackdown by the Tatmadaw, the armed forces. Opposition groups, including the exiled National Unity Government and many ethnic armed organizations, have called for a democratic federal state. By October 2023 the Tatmadaw controlled under 40% of the country. By May 2026 the [[United Nations]] refugee agency reported that around 299,000 people had fled to neighboring countries such as [[Bangladesh]], [[India]] and [[Thailand]].

Root-like structure of a [[Fungus|fungus]], consisting of a mass of branching, thread-like [[Hypha|hyphae]]. Mycelium may be too small to see, or may span thousands of acres, as in *Armillaria*. A fungus absorbs nutrients through its mycelium in two stages: the hyphae secrete enzymes that break food down into smaller units, which are then absorbed. Mycelia are vital to ecosystems for decomposing plant material, and their growth releases [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] into the atmosphere. Mycorrhizal mycelium increases the efficiency of water and nutrient absorption for most plants. Mycelium grown on agricultural waste can be used to produce alternatives to [[Polystyrene|polystyrene]] packaging and artificial leather. Fungi can eradicate some pollutants, such as [[Petroleum|petroleum]] products and some pesticides, in a process called mycoremediation.

Last phase of the [[Bronze Age]] in ancient Greece, c. 1750–1050 BC, and the first advanced, distinctively Greek civilization on the mainland. Its palatial states, named for the prominent site of Mycenae, included Pylos, Tiryns, Midea, Thebes and [[Athens]]. The Mycenaeans were stimulated by contact with [[Crete|Minoan Crete]] and traded across the Mediterranean. A warrior elite ruled palace-centered states under a king called the wanax. Their syllabic script, Linear B, offers the first written records of the Greek language. Their religion included several deities later found in the Olympic pantheon. The civilization collapsed into the Greek Dark Ages, with proposed causes including the Dorian invasion, the [[Sea Peoples]] and natural disasters. Its world became the setting of much ancient Greek literature, including the Trojan Epic Cycle.

Branch of biology concerned with the study of [[Fungus|fungi]], including their taxonomy, genetics, biochemical properties and use by humans. Fungi can be a source of tinder, food, [[Traditional medicine|traditional medicine]] and infection. [[Yeast|Yeasts]] are among the most heavily used fungi, particularly in food manufacturing. Mycology overlaps with phytopathology, the study of plant diseases, because most [[Pathogen|plant pathogens]] are fungi. Some fungi produce [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]], such as [[Penicillin]], and others serve as biological control agents against crop diseases. Many fungi break down lignin, a durable component of wood, and so play a critical role in the global carbon cycle. Field meetings to find fungi are called "forays". A biologist who specializes in fungi is called a mycologist.

Eye condition in which light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina, also called nearsightedness. Myopia usually results from an eyeball that grows too long, and distant objects appear blurred. Severe myopia raises the risk of macular degeneration, retinal detachment, cataracts and [[Glaucoma|glaucoma]]. It is corrected with [[Glasses|glasses]], contact lenses or refractive [[Surgery|surgery]]. Myopia is the most common eye disorder, affecting an estimated 1.5 billion people (22% of the world population), and rates have increased since the 1950s. Onset is often in school children, with worsening between the ages of 8 and 15.

Subphylum of terrestrial [[Arthropod|arthropods]], including [[Millipede|millipedes]] and [[Centipede|centipedes]]. The group contains about 13,000 species, all of them terrestrial. Molecular evidence and [[Fossil|fossils]] suggest diversification in the [[Cambrian]] period, and trace fossils show myriapods inhabited land by the [[Ordovician]]. The oldest known body fossil dates to approximately 427.0 ± 4.5 million years ago. Most species are detritivores that break down decaying plant material in moist forests, while centipedes are chiefly nocturnal [[Predation|predators]]. Millipedes have body segments fused in pairs, so each appears to bear two pairs of legs. The phylogenetic classification of myriapods is still debated.

American film, television, and stage actress. Known for adapting to her screen partner's acting style, she began in [[Silent film|silent films]] and was originally typecast in exotic roles. Her career improved after she played Nora Charles in *The Thin Man* (1934), a role she reprised five more times. Her performances peaked in the 1940s, including in *The Best Years of Our Lives*. She appeared in eight films between 1960 and 1981 before retiring. Although never nominated for an Academy Award, she received an Honorary Academy Award in 1991. She also worked for the Red Cross during [[World War II]]. In 2009, [[The Guardian]] named her one of the best actors never nominated for an Academy Award.

Myrtle family of dicotyledonous [[Plant|plants]] in the order Myrtales, including myrtle, [[Clove|clove]], [[Guava|guava]], allspice and [[Eucalyptus|eucalyptus]]. All species are woody and contain essential oils, and their flowers typically have parts in fours or fives. The leaves are evergreen and usually entire. A 2016 paper estimated about 5,950 species in about 132 genera, with a wide distribution in tropical and warm-temperate regions. Pollen fossils have been sourced to [[Gondwana]], and the breakup of that supercontinent during the [[Cretaceous]] isolated lineages that then diversified rapidly. Eucalyptus is nearly ubiquitous in the moister parts of [[Australia]], and *Eucalyptus regnans* is the tallest flowering plant in the world.

City in the southern Indian state of [[Karnataka]], officially renamed Mysuru in 2014 (metropolitan pop., 2023: 1,288,000). It is the administrative headquarters of Mysore district. As the traditional seat of the Wadiyar dynasty, it was the capital of the Kingdom of Mysore for almost six centuries (1399 to 1947), and its palaces earned it the nickname City of Palaces. The annual Dasara festival draws hundreds of thousands of [[Tourism|tourists]]. [[Hyder Ali]] and [[Tipu Sultan]] promoted mulberry cultivation and [[Silk|silk]] production in the region and fought four wars against the British. The city lies at 770 m (2,530 ft) at the foothills of the Chamundi Hills, about 140 km southwest of [[Bengaluru]].

American [[Social networking service|social networking service]], launched in August 2003. It was the first social network to reach a global audience and was the largest social networking site in the world from 2005 to 2009. News Corporation bought it for $580 million in 2005. At its peak in April 2008, it had 115 million monthly visitors. In May 2009, [[Facebook]] surpassed it in unique U.S. visitors, and its user base declined steadily afterward. [[Justin Timberlake]] and Specific Media bought it in 2011 for approximately $35 million. It had seven million monthly visitors as of 2019.

Subjective experience, also called spiritual or sacred experience, that is interpreted within a religious framework. In a strict sense, the term refers to an ecstatic unitive experience, or nonduality, of self and other objects. The concept developed in the 19th century as a defense against growing rationalism. [[William James]] popularized it in *The Varieties of Religious Experience* and identified four qualities: ineffability, noetic quality, transiency and passivity. [[Aldous Huxley]] and James held that mystical experiences share a common core. From the 1970s, a constructionist approach became dominant, holding that experiences are shaped by pre-existing frames of reference.

Religious traditions of human transformation aided by various practices and religious experiences. Popularly, mysticism means an ecstatic unitive experience of becoming one with God or the Absolute. Since the 1970s, scholars have noted that it can also mean insight into ultimate or hidden truths, as in Buddhist awakening, or altered states such as samadhi. The word derives from the Greek *múō*, meaning "to close" or "to conceal". In early Christianity it referred to the biblical, liturgical and contemplative dimensions of faith. Mystical traditions appear in [[Christianity]], [[Judaism]], [[Sufism]], [[Buddhism]], [[Hinduism]] and [[Western esotericism]].

headword: Mythologies of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas
sort_key: mythologies of the indigenous peoples of the americas
entry: Narratives, beliefs and sacred oral traditions of the [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas]], which differ widely by region. North American myths commonly feature a close relation to nature and animals, a belief in a Great Spirit, and [[Creation myth|creation stories]]. Animals often shape-shift, and marriages between humans and bears are common. Tricksters such as [[Coyote (mythology)|Coyote]] and the Plains figure Old Man provide humor and moral lessons. Many myths were transcribed by ethnologists in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. In Mesoamerica, the Olmec, Maya and Aztec developed pantheons such as the Feathered Serpent Quetzalcoatl. In the Andes, the Inca creator god Viracocha shaped humanity from stone at Lake Titicaca.

Independent agency of the U.S. federal government responsible for the civil space program and aeronautics research. Established in 1958 amid the [[Space Race]], it succeeded the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics and has led most American spaceflight programs, including Project Mercury, the Apollo program, [[Skylab]], the [[Space Shuttle]], the [[International Space Station]] and the ongoing Artemis program. The [[Apollo 11]] Moon landing took place in 1969. Its science programs include the [[Hubble Space Telescope]], the [[James Webb Space Telescope]] and robotic missions such as New Horizons. Headquartered in [[Washington, D.C.]], it operates ten field centers. Its fiscal year 2026 budget was authorized at $24.4 billion.

Company that sanctions and operates [[Auto racing|stock car racing]] in the United States. Founded by Bill France Sr. in 1948, it is headquartered in Daytona Beach, Florida, and sanctions over 1,500 races a year at more than 100 tracks in 48 U.S. states, as well as in Canada, Mexico, Brazil and Europe. Its roots lie in moonshine runners who raced against each other during Prohibition. The Cup Series is its top division. Richard Petty holds the Cup Series win record with 200, and he shares the championship record of seven titles with Dale Earnhardt and Jimmie Johnson.

Intergovernmental military alliance of 32 member states, established with the North Atlantic Treaty of 1949. Under Article 5 of the treaty, an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all. NATO was formed to counter the [[Soviet Union]], whose rival [[Warsaw Pact]] formed in 1955. After the [[Cold War]], it first intervened in the [[Bosnian War]] (1992–1995) and bombed Yugoslavia during the Kosovo War in 1999. Article 5 was invoked for the first and only time after the September 11 attacks, leading to involvement in the [[War in Afghanistan (2001–2021)|war in Afghanistan]]. Russia's 2022 invasion of [[Ukraine]] led [[Finland]] and Sweden to join. Members have committed to spending at least 5% of gross domestic product on defense by 2035. Its headquarters are in [[Brussels]], Belgium.

American commercial broadcast television network and flagship property of NBCUniversal, a subsidiary of [[Comcast]]. Founded in 1926 by the Radio Corporation of America, it was co-owned by [[General Electric]], Westinghouse, AT&T and [[United Fruit Company]]. In 1932, the U.S. government forced General Electric to sell RCA and NBC because of antitrust violations. NBC pioneered commercial television in 1939 and introduced color television in 1953. It is the oldest of the traditional Big Three networks, along with ABC and [[CBS]]. Its headquarters are in [[New York City]] at Rockefeller Center. Long-running programs include *Meet the Press* (1947), *Today* (1952) and [[Saturday Night Live]] (1975).

Hazard-labeling standard of the U.S.-based National Fire Protection Association, used on placards for hazardous materials. Its Safety Square, or fire diamond, has four colored sections: red for flammability, blue for health hazards, yellow for reactivity and white for special hazards. Ratings for the first three run from 0 (no reasonable hazard) to 4 (severe hazard), using [[Arabic numerals]]. The standard was prompted by a 1959 fire at the Charlotte Chemical Company, where firefighters unaware that a vat held metallic [[Sodium|sodium]] attempted to suppress it, causing an explosion that injured 13 firefighters. It was first tentatively adopted in 1960.

American nonprofit public broadcasting organization, headquartered in Washington, D.C. It syndicates news and cultural programming to more than 1,000 public radio stations. Its flagship drive-time programs, *Morning Edition* and *All Things Considered*, are among the most popular radio programs in the United States. NPR replaced the National Educational Radio Network in 1970 under the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967, signed by [[Lyndon B. Johnson]]. Its first broadcast, on April 20, 1971, covered [[United States Senate|Senate]] hearings on the [[Vietnam War]]. Funding comes from member station dues, corporate underwriting and, until 2025, grants from the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. Its content is also available as [[Podcast|podcasts]].

American vocal pop boy band formed by Chris Kirkpatrick in [[Orlando, Florida]] in 1995. Its members were Kirkpatrick, JC Chasez, Joey Fatone, [[Justin Timberlake]] and Lance Bass. The album *No Strings Attached* (2000) sold 2.4 million copies in its first week in the U.S., a record for over fifteen years. The group went on indefinite hiatus in 2002 and briefly reunited in 2023. It completed five nationwide tours, sold over 70 million records and performed at the [[Super Bowl]].

Capital and largest city of [[Chad]], at the confluence of the Chari and Logone rivers (urban pop., 2025: 1,723,000). Founded as Fort-Lamy by French commander Émile Gentil on May 29, 1900, it was renamed N'Djamena in 1973 by President François Tombalbaye, after a nearby Arabic village whose name means "place of rest". Meat, fish and cotton processing are its chief industries, and it is a regional market for livestock, salt, dates and grains. It forms a transborder agglomeration with Kousséri, in [[Cameroon]], across the rivers.
